questions.text: Which of the following constitutes electric current in metallic conductors?

key_points: In metallic conductors, free electrons are the charge carriers
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Flow of electrons
rubric.hint: Think about which particles are free to move in a metallic conductor.

questions.text: The potential difference between two points is 1 V. This means:

options.text: 1 J of work moves 2 C of charge
1 C of charge gains 1 J of energy
2 J of work moves 1 C of charge
1 C of charge loses 2 J of energy

key_points: V = W/Q; when V=1V and Q=1C, W=1J
rubric.expected_answer: (b) 1 C of charge gains 1 J of energy
rubric.hint: Use V = W/Q; substitute V=1 and Q=1 to find work done.

questions.text: Define electric current. Write the formula relating charge, current and time. State the SI unit of current and define it.

key_points: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a cross-section of a conductor
1 A = flow of 1 C charge per second
rubric.expected_answer: Electric current is defined as the amount of electric charge (Q) flowing through a conductor in unit time (t). I = Q/t. SI unit is ampere (A). 1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second (1 A = 1 C/s).
rubric.hint: Define current as rate of charge flow; recall I = Q/t and 1 A.

questions.text: What is meant by potential difference between two points in a circuit? Define 1 volt.

key_points: PD between two points = work done to move unit positive charge from one point to the other
1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹)
rubric.expected_answer: Potential difference between two points is the work done in moving a unit positive charge from one point to the other. V = W/Q. 1 volt is the PD when 1 joule of work is done to move 1 coulomb of charge from one point to the other.
rubric.hint: Define PD as work per unit charge; use V = W/Q for 1 volt.

questions.text: A current of 0.5 A is drawn by a filament of an electric bulb for 10 minutes. Find the amount of electric charge that flows through the circuit.

key_points: Given: I = 0.5 A, t = 10 min = 600 s
rubric.hint: Use Q = It; convert minutes to seconds first.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): In an electric circuit, the direction of conventional current is from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the cell through the external circuit.
Reason (R): Electrons, being negatively charged, flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal of the cell.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

key_points: Conventional current flows from + to - externally, opposite to electron flow
Electron flow (- to + externally) causes conventional current (+ to - externally)
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Electrons flow from - to + terminal; conventional current is defined as opposite, i.e., + to - through external circuit.
rubric.hint: Conventional current is opposite to the direction of electron flow.

questions.text: According to Ohm's law (at constant temperature), the potential difference V across a conductor is:

key_points: Ohm's law: V ∝ I at constant temperature, i.e., V = IR
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Directly proportional to current I
rubric.hint: Think about how V and I relate at constant temperature (Ohm's law).

questions.text: The resistance of a wire is doubled and simultaneously the potential difference across it is also doubled. The current through the wire:

key_points: I = V/R; if both V and R double, I = 2V/2R = V/R — unchanged
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Remains the same. I_new = 2V/2R = V/R = I_original
rubric.hint: Apply I = V/R; see what happens when both V and R are doubled.

questions.text: State Ohm's law. Write its mathematical expression and define resistance. State the SI unit of resistance.

key_points: Statement: V across a conductor ∝ I through it, at constant temperature
SI unit of resistance is ohm (Ω)
rubric.expected_answer: Ohm's law: The potential difference across the ends of a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the current through it, provided temperature remains constant. Mathematically: V = IR, where R is resistance. SI unit of resistance is ohm (Ω). 1 Ω = 1 V / 1 A.
rubric.hint: State Ohm's law, write V = IR, define R, and give its SI unit.

questions.text: List the factors on which the resistance of a conductor depends. Write the expression R = ρl/A and define each term with its SI unit.

key_points: Resistance depends on: (i) length l — directly proportional
(ii) area of cross-section A — inversely proportional
R = ρl/A; ρ = resistivity (Ω m); l = length (m); A = area (m²)
rubric.expected_answer: Resistance depends on (i) length l: R ∝ l (ii) area A: R ∝ 1/A (iii) nature of material: characterised by resistivity ρ (iv) temperature. Combined: R = ρl/A, where ρ = electrical resistivity (SI unit Ω m), l = length (m), A = cross-sectional area (m²).
rubric.hint: Use R = rho*l/A; describe how R changes with length, area, and material.

questions.text: Why are coils of electric toasters and electric irons made of an alloy rather than a pure metal? Give two reasons.

key_points: Alloys have higher resistivity than pure metals — produce more heat for same current
Alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures — more durable
Alloys have high melting point — do not melt easily under high temperatures
rubric.expected_answer: Alloys are preferred because: (1) They have higher resistivity than pure metals, so they produce more heat for the same current. (2) They do not oxidise (corrode) readily at high temperatures and have high melting points, making them more durable. Example: Nichrome (alloy of Ni, Cr, Mn, Fe).
rubric.hint: Think why high resistivity and high melting point matter for heating elements.

questions.text: The potential difference between the terminals of an electric heater is 60 V when it draws a current of 4 A from the source. What current will the heater draw if the potential difference is increased to 120 V?

rubric.hint: Find R = V/I first; then apply Ohm's law at the new voltage.

questions.text:
Study the V–I graph in Figure A showing two metallic wires A and B connected in the same circuit at different times.
(a) Which wire has greater resistance? Give reason.
(b) Calculate the resistance of wire A from the graph.
(c) State what happens to the current through wire B if the potential difference across it is doubled.

key_points: (a) Wire B has greater resistance — steeper slope means more V per unit I, i.e., greater R
(b) R_A = V/I = 8.0 V / 2.0 A = 4 Ω (reading from graph at any point on line A)
(c) Current through B doubles — Ohm's law: I ∝ V at constant R
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Wire B. Steeper slope on V-I graph → higher R = V/I. (b) From graph, at I=2A, V_A=8V → R_A = 8/2 = 4 Ω. (c) Current doubles, since I = V/R and R is constant.
rubric.hint: On a V-I graph, slope = R; steeper slope means higher resistance.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent pure metals.
Reason (R): Alloys are used in heating elements because they do not oxidise readily at high temperatures.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

key_points: A is TRUE — alloys like nichrome have higher resistivity than pure metals
R is TRUE — alloys resist oxidation at high temperatures
R is NOT the explanation for A — high resistivity and resistance to oxidation are independent properties of alloys
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A. The higher resistivity is a separate property from oxidation resistance.
rubric.hint: Both statements are true; check if oxidation resistance explains high resistivity.

questions.text: A piece of wire of resistance R is cut into five equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel. If the equivalent resistance of this combination is R′, then the ratio R/R′ is:

rubric.expected_answer: (d) 25. Each piece = R/5; five in parallel: R' = (R/5)/5 = R/25; R/R' = 25.
rubric.hint: Each piece is R/5; apply parallel formula 1/Rp = n/R_each, then find R/Rp.

questions.text: When several resistors are connected in series in a circuit, which physical quantity remains the same through all resistors?

key_points: In series, current I is the same through every component
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Current. In a series circuit, there is only one path for current flow.
rubric.hint: In series there is one path; think which quantity is shared by all resistors.

questions.text: When three resistors R₁, R₂ and R₃ are connected in series, derive the expression for their equivalent resistance Rs using Ohm's law.

key_points: Same current I flows through all
Total PD: V = V1 + V2 + V3 = IR1 + IR2 + IR3 = I(R1+R2+R3)
rubric.expected_answer: In series, same current I flows through all resistors. V = V1+V2+V3 = IR1+IR2+IR3 = I(R1+R2+R3). Since V = I·Rs, we get Rs = R1+R2+R3.
rubric.hint: In series same I flows; write V = I(R1+R2+R3) to derive Rs.

questions.text: State two advantages of connecting electrical devices in parallel rather than in series in household circuits.

key_points: Each device operates at the same (full) voltage
Each device can be switched on/off independently
Failure of one device does not affect others
Each device can draw the current it needs
rubric.expected_answer: (1) Each device gets the same full supply voltage and can be operated independently. (2) If one device fails/is switched off, others continue to work unaffected.
rubric.hint: Full supply voltage and independent operation are key advantages of parallel connection.

questions.text: Show how you would connect three resistors, each of resistance 6 Ω, so that the combination has a resistance of (i) 9 Ω and (ii) 4 Ω. Justify your answer with calculations.

key_points: (i) 9 Ω: Two resistors (6+6=12Ω) in parallel with third (6Ω) gives: 1/R = 1/12 + 1/6 = 3/12 → R=4Ω — NO
(i) 9 Ω: Two in parallel (3Ω) in series with one (6Ω) = 9 Ω ✓
(ii) 4 Ω: Two in parallel (3Ω) in series with one (6Ω) = 9Ω — NO
(i) 9 Ω: Correct: two 6Ω in parallel = 3Ω; 3Ω + 6Ω in series = 9Ω
(ii) 4 Ω: Correct: one 6Ω in series with another 6Ω gives 12Ω; 12Ω in parallel with 6Ω: 1/R=1/12+1/6=3/12 → R=4Ω
rubric.expected_answer: (i) 9 Ω: Connect two 6Ω resistors in parallel (Rp = 6×6/(6+6) = 3Ω), then connect this combination in series with the third 6Ω resistor. R = 3+6 = 9Ω. (ii) 4Ω: Connect two 6Ω in series (Rs=12Ω), then connect this in parallel with the third 6Ω: 1/R=1/12+1/6=3/12, R=4Ω.
rubric.hint: Try two-parallel-one-series for 9 ohm; two-series-one-parallel for 4 ohm.

questions.text: An electric lamp whose resistance is 20 Ω, and a conductor of 4 Ω resistance are connected to a 6 V battery in series. Calculate: (a) the total resistance of the circuit, (b) the current through the circuit, and (c) the potential difference across the electric lamp and across the conductor.

rubric.formula: Rs = R1+R2; I = V/Rs; V = IR
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Rs = 24 Ω (b) I = 0.25 A (c) V_lamp = 5 V, V_conductor = 1 V
rubric.hint: Add R for total, use I = V/Rs, then V = IR across each component.

questions.text:
Study Figure A, which shows three resistors R₁ = 2 Ω, R₂ = 3 Ω and R₃ = 6 Ω connected in parallel to a 6 V battery.
(a) Calculate the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination.
(b) Find the current through each resistor.
(c) Find the total current drawn from the battery.

key_points: Total I = 3+2+1 = 6 A (also: I = V/Rp = 6/1 = 6 A)
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Rp = 1 Ω (b) I1=3A, I2=2A, I3=1A (c) Total I=6A
rubric.hint: Use 1/Rp = 1/R1+1/R2+1/R3; each branch current = 6 V divided by R.

questions.text:
Study Figure B, which shows R₁ = 5 Ω connected in series with a parallel combination of R₂ = 10 Ω and R₃ = 20 Ω, all connected to a 12 V battery.
(a) Find the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of R₂ and R₃.
(b) Find the total resistance of the circuit.
(c) Find the total current from the battery.
(d) Find the current through R₂.

rubric.hint: Find Rp for parallel pair first, add to R1, then use I = V/R_total.

questions.text: Derive the expression for the equivalent resistance when three resistors R₁, R₂ and R₃ are connected in parallel. Draw a labelled circuit diagram. Show that the equivalent resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance.

key_points: In parallel: same PD (V) across each resistor
Diagram: battery, 3 parallel branches each with Ri
Rp < R1, R2, R3 individually (since 1/Rp > 1/Ri for each i)
rubric.expected_answer: Derivation with diagram. In parallel: V same across all. I=I1+I2+I3. I1=V/R1, I2=V/R2, I3=V/R3. V/Rp = V/R1+V/R2+V/R3 → 1/Rp=1/R1+1/R2+1/R3. Since 1/Rp > 1/R1 (adding positive terms), Rp < R1.
rubric.hint: In parallel same V appears across all; write I = V/R1+V/R2+V/R3 to derive 1/Rp.

questions.text: An electric lamp of 100 Ω, a toaster of resistance 50 Ω and a water filter of resistance 500 Ω are connected in parallel to a 220 V source. Find: (a) the equivalent resistance of the combination, (b) the total current drawn from the source.

rubric.hint: Use 1/Rp = 1/100+1/50+1/500 to find Rp, then I = 220/Rp.

questions.text: Two conducting wires of the same material, equal lengths and equal diameters are first connected in series and then in parallel in a circuit across the same potential difference. The ratio of heat produced in the series combination to that in the parallel combination is:

key_points: Let each wire = R. Series: Rs = 2R; H_s = V²t/(2R)
rubric.hint: Use H = V2t/R for each configuration and compare at the same supply voltage.

questions.text: State Joule's law of heating. Write the mathematical expression H = I²Rt, explaining the meaning of each symbol and the three relationships implied by the law.

key_points: H in joules (J), I in amperes (A), R in ohms (Ω), t in seconds (s)
rubric.expected_answer: Joule's law: The heat produced in a resistor is (i) directly proportional to the square of current (H∝I²), (ii) directly proportional to resistance (H∝R), and (iii) directly proportional to time (H∝t). Combined: H = I²Rt (J = A²·Ω·s).
rubric.hint: State H = I2Rt; identify each symbol and list the three proportionalities.

questions.text: Why does the cord of an electric heater not glow while the heating element does? What properties should a good heating element possess?

key_points: Cord has very low resistance (copper/aluminium) — less heat produced
Heating element has high resistance (alloy like nichrome) — more heat
Good heating element: high resistivity, high melting point, does not oxidise
rubric.expected_answer: The cord has low resistance so very little heat is produced (H=I²Rt, small R). The heating element (nichrome) has high resistance and produces large heat. A good heating element needs: (1) high resistivity, (2) high melting point, (3) resistance to oxidation at high temperatures.
rubric.hint: Compare H = I2Rt for cord (low R) and element (high R).

questions.text: Explain the working of an electric fuse. Why is it connected in series in a circuit? If an electric iron of 1 kW is operated at 220 V, what current rating fuse should be used?

key_points: Fuse wire has low melting point alloy
In series — all current passes through it
Excess current heats fuse → melts → breaks circuit → protects appliance
I = P/V = 1000/220 = 4.54 A → use 5 A fuse
rubric.expected_answer: Fuse: low-melting alloy wire in series with circuit. Excess current raises temperature, melts fuse, breaks circuit. Must be in series so all current flows through it. For 1kW at 220V: I = 1000/220 = 4.54A → 5A fuse required.
rubric.hint: Fuse melts by Joule heating; use I = P/V to find the operating current.

questions.text: An electric iron of resistance 20 Ω takes a current of 5 A. Calculate the heat developed in 30 seconds.

rubric.hint: Apply H = I2Rt directly with the given I, R, and t values.

questions.text:
(a) Derive Joule's law of heating (H = I²Rt) from energy considerations.
(b) An electric iron consumes energy at a rate of 840 W when heating is at the maximum rate and 360 W when at minimum. The voltage is 220 V. Find the current and resistance in each case.

key_points: Derivation: Work done = VQ = V(It) = VIt; by Ohm's law V=IR, H=I²Rt
rubric.formula: H = I²Rt; P = VI; I = P/V; R = V/I
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Source does work W=VQ=VIt on charge Q=It. Since V=IR, W=I²Rt. This appears as heat H=I²Rt. (b) I_max=3.82A, R_max=57.6Ω; I_min=1.64A, R_min=134.15Ω.
rubric.hint: Derive H=I2Rt from W=VIt and V=IR; for part b use I=P/V.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT represent electrical power in a circuit?

key_points: P = VI = I²R = V²/R. IR² has dimensions of V·Ω = V²/A which is not watts
rubric.expected_answer: (b) IR². The correct expressions for power are VI, I²R and V²/R. IR² does not have units of power.
rubric.hint: Check each option against P = VI = I2R = V2/R for correct dimensions.

questions.text: An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. When it is operated on 110 V, the power consumed will be:

rubric.hint: Find R = V2/P at rated voltage; then use P = V2/R at 110 V.

questions.text: Define electric power. Write three equivalent expressions for electric power in terms of V, I, and R. State the SI unit and define it. What is 1 kWh?

key_points: Power = rate of electrical energy consumption
SI unit: watt (W); 1 W = 1 V × 1 A
rubric.expected_answer: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed. P = VI = I²R = V²/R. SI unit is watt (W); 1W = 1J/s. 1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J is the commercial unit (unit of electricity).
rubric.hint: Define power as rate of energy use; write P = VI = I2R = V2/R.

questions.text: An electric refrigerator rated 400 W operates 8 hours per day. Calculate: (a) the energy consumed in 30 days in kWh, and (b) the cost of this energy at Rs 3.00 per kWh.

key_points: Energy = Power × time = 400 W × 8 h/day × 30 days = 96,000 Wh = 96 kWh
rubric.hint: Energy (kWh) = Power (kW) x time (h); multiply kWh by cost per unit.

questions.text:
Two lamps, one rated 100 W at 220 V and the other 60 W at 220 V, are connected in parallel to a 220 V mains supply.
(a) Calculate the resistance of each lamp.
(b) Find the current through each lamp.
(c) Which lamp glows brighter and why?
(d) Find the total current drawn from the supply.
(e) Find the energy consumed by each lamp in 8 hours.

key_points: (c) 100W lamp glows brighter as it consumes more power
rubric.hint: Parallel: same voltage; use R = V2/P and I = P/V for each lamp.

questions.text: A charge of 180 C passes through a wire in 1 minute. The current in the wire is:

rubric.hint: Use I = Q/t; convert 1 minute to seconds before dividing.

questions.text: The potential difference between two points in a circuit is 1 V. This means:

options.text: 1 J of work is done to move 1 C of charge between the points
1 C of charge moves between the points in 1 second
1 A of current flows between the points
1 W of power is dissipated between the points

key_points: V = W/Q. If V = 1 V, then W = 1 J per coulomb.
rubric.expected_answer: (a). 1 volt means 1 joule of work per coulomb of charge.
rubric.hint: Use V = W/Q; if V=1 and Q=1 C, how much work is done?

questions.text: Define electric current. What is its SI unit? Name and state the device used to measure it.

key_points: Electric current = rate of flow of electric charge; I = Q/t
Measured by ammeter connected in series
rubric.expected_answer: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor. I = Q/t. SI unit is ampere (A). It is measured by an ammeter connected in series in the circuit.
rubric.hint: Define current as rate of charge flow; name the ammeter connected in series.

questions.text: Calculate the charge that flows through a wire when a current of {I} A is maintained for {t} seconds. Also find the number of electrons that pass through the cross-section. (charge on electron = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

rubric.expected_answer: Q = {I} × {t} = {Q} C; n = {Q}/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) = {n} electrons.
rubric.hint: Use Q = It, then n = Q divided by electron charge.

questions.text: Why do we use a voltmeter in parallel and an ammeter in series in a circuit? What would happen if their positions were interchanged?

key_points: Voltmeter has very high resistance → negligible current drawn → measures PD without disturbing circuit
Ammeter has very low resistance → negligible voltage drop across it → measures current without disturbing circuit
If interchanged: voltmeter in series → circuit nearly broken (very high R, no significant current); ammeter in parallel → nearly short circuits the component
rubric.expected_answer: Voltmeter in parallel: its high resistance ensures it draws negligible current. Ammeter in series: its low resistance causes negligible voltage drop. If interchanged, voltmeter in series would block current (near open circuit); ammeter in parallel would short the component.
rubric.hint: Voltmeter has very high R (parallel); ammeter has very low R (series).

questions.text: The graph between voltage (V) and current (I) for a metallic conductor at constant temperature is:

options.text: A straight line through the origin
A straight line not through the origin

key_points: By Ohm's law V = IR ⇒ V ∝ I at constant T, so the V-I graph is a straight line through the origin.
rubric.expected_answer: (a) A straight line through the origin.
rubric.hint: V proportional to I at constant temperature; what shape does V-I graph have?

questions.text: If the length of a wire is doubled and its cross-sectional area is halved, its resistance becomes:

rubric.expected_answer: (c) 4 times. R ∝ L/A ⇒ R′ = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4R.
rubric.hint: Apply R = rho*L/A with L doubled and A halved to find the net effect.

questions.text: State Ohm's law. Under what conditions does a conductor obey Ohm's law?

key_points: Ohm's law: V ∝ I, i.e., V = IR, at constant temperature and unchanged physical conditions
rubric.expected_answer: Ohm's law: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. V = IR.
rubric.hint: State V = IR and specify the condition of constant temperature.

questions.text: On what factors does the resistance of a conductor depend? Write the formula relating resistance to these factors.

key_points: R = ρL/A where ρ is resistivity of the material
rubric.expected_answer: Resistance depends on: (1) length L (R ∝ L), (2) area of cross-section A (R ∝ 1/A), (3) material (ρ). Formula: R = ρL/A where ρ is resistivity (unit: Ω·m).
rubric.hint: Use R = rho*L/A; describe how R depends on length, area, and resistivity.

questions.text: A student draws a V-I graph for two wires P and Q. Wire P has a steeper slope than wire Q. Which wire has higher resistance? How do you know from the graph?

key_points: In a V-I graph, slope = V/I = R
rubric.formula: R = V/I = slope of V-I graph
rubric.expected_answer: Wire P has higher resistance. In a V-I graph, the slope = V/I = R. A steeper slope means higher resistance.
rubric.hint: Slope of V-I graph = V/I = R; steeper slope means higher resistance.

questions.text: Why are alloys such as nichrome, manganin, and constantan preferred for making resistance wires in heating elements and standard resistors?

key_points: High resistivity → short length needed for desired resistance
Do not oxidise (corrode) readily at high temperatures
Low temperature coefficient of resistance → resistance stays stable
rubric.expected_answer: Alloys like nichrome have (1) high resistivity, so short lengths give desired R; (2) do not oxidise at high temperatures; (3) low temperature coefficient, so resistance is stable over temperature changes.
rubric.hint: Alloys have high resistivity and resist oxidation; explain why each property matters.

questions.text: A potential difference of {V} V is applied across a resistor of {R} Ω. Calculate (a) the current through the resistor, (b) the charge that flows through it in {t} seconds.

rubric.hint: Use I = V/R for current, then Q = I times t for charge.

questions.text: Three resistors of 3 Ω, 6 Ω and 9 Ω are connected in series. Their equivalent resistance is:

rubric.hint: In series Rs = R1+R2+R3; simply add all three resistance values.

questions.text: Three identical resistors each of resistance R are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance of the combination is:

rubric.hint: Apply 1/Rp = 3/R for three equal resistors in parallel, then invert.

questions.text: In a parallel circuit, if one branch is disconnected, the current in the remaining branches:

key_points: In parallel, each branch has the same PD. Disconnecting one branch does not change the PD across others, so their currents are unchanged.
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Remains unchanged. Each branch independently has the same supply voltage, so disconnecting one does not affect others.
rubric.hint: In parallel each branch has the same independent voltage.

questions.text: Distinguish between series and parallel combinations of resistors: give one similarity and two differences.

key_points: Similarity: total resistance can be calculated in both cases using standard formulas
Series: same current; PD divides; Rs = R1+R2+... (Rs > any individual R)
Parallel: same PD; current divides; Rp < smallest individual R
rubric.expected_answer: Similarity: both obey Ohm's law as a combination. Differences: (1) Series — same current, PD divides; Parallel — same PD, current divides. (2) In series Rs > any single R; in parallel Rp < smallest R.
rubric.hint: Contrast series (same I) with parallel (same V) and compare equivalent R values.

questions.text: In the given circuit, three resistors R1 = 2 Ω, R2 = 3 Ω and R3 = 6 Ω are connected in parallel across a 6 V battery. Find: (a) the equivalent resistance, (b) the current through each resistor, (c) the total current from the battery.

rubric.expected_answer: (a) Rp = 1 Ω (b) I1=3A, I2=2A, I3=1A (c) I_total=6A
rubric.hint: Use 1/Rp = 1/2+1/3+1/6, then find each branch current from I = V/R.

questions.text: Explain why household electrical appliances are connected in parallel and not in series.

key_points: In parallel each device gets the full supply voltage (220 V)
Each device can be switched on/off independently
Failure of one device does not affect others
In series voltage would be divided and one failure stops all
rubric.expected_answer: In parallel: (1) each device gets full 220 V, (2) can be operated independently, (3) failure of one does not stop others. In series voltage divides and one break stops the whole circuit.
rubric.hint: Full supply voltage and independent switching are the two main parallel advantages.

questions.text: In the circuit shown, R1 = 5 Ω is connected in series with a parallel combination of R2 = 10 Ω and R3 = 20 Ω. The supply is 12 V. Find the total resistance and the current drawn from the supply.

rubric.formula: Rp = R2R3/(R2+R3); R_total = R1+Rp; I = V/R_total
rubric.hint: Find Rp = R2*R3/(R2+R3) first, add to R1, then use I = V/R_total.

questions.text: Two resistors of {R1} Ω and {R2} Ω are connected (a) in series and (b) in parallel across a {V} V supply. Find the equivalent resistance and current drawn from the supply in each case.

rubric.expected_answer: (a) Rs={Rs}Ω, Is={Is}A (b) Rp={Rp}Ω, Ip={Ip}A
rubric.hint: Series: Rs = R1+R2, I = V/Rs; parallel: Rp = R1*R2/(R1+R2), I = V/Rp.

questions.text: An electric heater draws 2 A from a 220 V supply. If it is used for 30 minutes, the heat produced is:

rubric.hint: Use H = VIt; convert 30 minutes to seconds first.

questions.text: Which of the following characteristics is NOT required for the material of a fuse wire?

key_points: Fuse wire needs: low melting point (melts at small excess current), high resistivity (significant heating at lower currents), appropriate thin cross-section
Low resistivity is NOT desired — the fuse must heat up quickly
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Low resistivity. Fuse needs HIGH resistivity to generate enough heat to melt at fault current.
rubric.hint: Fuse must heat and melt fast; think whether high or low resistivity does this.

questions.text: State Joule’s law of heating. On which factors does the heat produced in a conductor depend?

key_points: H ∝ t (time for which current flows)
rubric.expected_answer: Joule’s law: H = I²Rt. Heat depends on (1) square of current I, (2) resistance R, (3) time t.
rubric.hint: State H = I2Rt; list its three proportionalities with I squared, R, and t.

questions.text: Why is the filament of an electric bulb made of tungsten, while the connecting lead wires are made of copper?

key_points: Tungsten: very high melting point (~3380°C), can withstand temperature; high resistivity so it glows at the operating current
Copper: very low resistivity, negligible heat generated in lead wires, so energy is not wasted
rubric.expected_answer: Tungsten: high melting point and high resistivity → glows at high temp without melting. Copper: low resistivity → negligible heat in lead wires (no energy waste).
rubric.hint: Contrast high resistivity of tungsten with very low resistivity of copper.

questions.text: An electric iron is rated 750 W at 220 V. Calculate its resistance and the current it draws. How much heat energy is produced if it is used for 2 hours?

rubric.formula: R = V²/P; I = P/V; H = Pt
rubric.hint: Use R = V2/P, I = P/V, and H = Pt for the three parts.

questions.text: A 100 W bulb and a 40 W bulb are both designed for 220 V operation. When connected in series to a 220 V supply, which bulb will glow brighter?

key_points: In series, same current flows; P = I²R ⇒ higher R ⇒ more power
40 W bulb has higher resistance ⇒ dissipates more power in series ⇒ glows brighter
rubric.expected_answer: (b) 40 W bulb. In series, same I; P=I²R. R_40 > R_100, so 40W bulb dissipates more power.
rubric.hint: Series: same I; use R = V2/P for each bulb, then compare P = I2R.

questions.text: The SI unit of electrical energy consumed is:

key_points: SI unit of energy is joule (J). kWh is a commercial/practical unit, not the SI unit.
rubric.formula: E = Pt (in joules when P in W, t in s)
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Joule (J). kWh is a commercial unit; the SI unit of energy is joule.
rubric.hint: Distinguish the SI unit (joule) from the commercial unit (kWh) of energy.

questions.text: Define electric power. Write the three equivalent expressions for power in terms of V, I, and R. Give the SI unit.

key_points: Electric power = rate at which electrical energy is consumed/dissipated
SI unit: watt (W) = joule per second
rubric.expected_answer: Electric power is the rate of consumption of electrical energy. P = VI = I²R = V²/R. SI unit: watt (W).
rubric.hint: Define power as rate of energy use; write P = VI = I2R = V2/R.

questions.text: A household uses the following appliances daily: one 1000 W geyser for 1 hour, four 60 W bulbs for 5 hours, and one 500 W TV for 3 hours. If electricity costs Rs 5 per kWh, find the total daily energy consumed and daily cost.

rubric.formula: E = P × t (kWh); Cost = E × rate
rubric.expected_answer: Geyser 1000 Wh + Bulbs 1200 Wh + TV 1500 Wh = 3700 Wh = 3.7 kWh. Cost = 3.7 × 5 = Rs 18.50.
rubric.hint: Energy = P (kW) times time (h) per appliance; sum all, then multiply by rate.

questions.text:
Three resistors of 6 Ω, 3 Ω, and 2 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. The wire connecting the 2 Ω resistor feels hotter than the others after a few minutes.

(a) Calculate the equivalent resistance of the combination. [1]
(b) Find the current through the 2 Ω resistor. [1]
(c) Explain why the 2 Ω wire heats up more than the 6 Ω wire. [2]

key_points: Current through 6 Ω = 12/6 = 2 A; higher current in 2 Ω
H = I²Rt — greater current produces more heat in same time
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Req = 1 Ω. (b) I = 12/2 = 6 A. (c) In parallel all have same voltage (12 V); 2 Ω carries 6 A vs 2 A through 6 Ω. Since H = I²Rt, the 2 Ω wire dissipates more heat.
rubric.hint: In parallel all share the same voltage; use H = I2Rt to explain heating difference.

questions.text: An electric heater draws a current of 5 A from a 220 V supply. What is the power consumed by the heater?

key_points: Step 1: Use the formula P = V x I
rubric.hint: Use P = V times I with the given voltage and current.

questions.text: A 100 ohm resistance is connected across a 220 V supply. Calculate the power dissipated in the resistance.

key_points: Step 1: When only V and R are known, use P = V^2 / R
rubric.hint: Only V and R are known; use P = V2/R.

questions.text: A current of 4 A flows through a 25 ohm resistor. Find the power dissipated as heat.

key_points: Step 1: When only I and R are known, use P = I^2 x R
rubric.hint: Only I and R are known; use P = I2 times R.

questions.text: An electric bulb is rated 60 W at 220 V. Find (i) the resistance of the filament and (ii) the current flowing through it when connected to a 220 V supply.

key_points: Step 2 (current): P = V x I  =>  I = P / V = 60 / 220
rubric.hint: Use R = V2/P and I = P/V at the rated voltage.

questions.text: A household uses the following electrical appliances: (i) Refrigerator of 400 W for 10 hours per day. (ii) Two electric fans of 80 W each for 12 hours per day. (iii) 6 electric tubes of 18 W each for 6 hours per day. Calculate the total electrical energy consumed by the household in one day in kWh.

key_points: Two fans: 2 x 0.08 kW x 12 h = 1.92 kWh
Six tubes: 6 x 0.018 kW x 6 h = 0.648 kWh
Final: Total energy consumed = 6.568 kWh per day
rubric.expected_answer: Total energy = 6.568 kWh per day
rubric.hint: Compute Energy = P (kW) times hours for each appliance, then sum in kWh.
